abstract: Somatic mutations accumulate in the liver during aging, yet their role in chronic liver disease (CLD) remains unclear due to the difficulty of obtaining liver tissue for analysis. Here, we demonstrate that circulating cell-free DNA (cfDNA) can be used as a minimally invasive tool to detect liver-derived somatic mutations in patients with CLD. Using ultra-deep targeted duplex sequencing, we show that CLD patients have a higher mutation burden in CLD-associated somatic mutation (CASM) genes compared to healthy individuals. Recurrent driver mutations, including CHD4, INSR, and GPAM, were detected in both liver tissue and cfDNA, with distinct mutational patterns linked to disease etiology: INSR mutations were enriched in metabolic-dysfunction associated steatotic liver disease, while GPAM mutations were associated with alcohol-related liver disease. Liver transplantation led to a significant reduction in CASM mutation burden in cfDNA, providing strong evidence for the diseased-liver origin of these mutations. These findings establish cfDNA analysis as a scalable and noninvasive platform for investigating somatic evolution in non-malignant tissues, offering new opportunities for molecular stratification, longitudinal monitoring, and early detection of CLD progression.
